chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn Idris (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: My father narrated to us from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ali ibn Asbat, from Malik ibn Masma' ibn Malik, from Sama'a ibn Mihran, from Abu Abdillah al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both). He said:
He said: O Sama'a! A believer will never be free from four trials: a neighbor who harms him, a devil who leads him astray, a hypocrite who follows his tracks, and a believer who envies him.

I said: May I be your sacrifice! A believer who envies him? He said: O Sama'a! Know that he is the most severe of them against him. I said: And how is that? He said: Because he says something about him, and he is believed in that.

key_terms.يَحْسُدُ: To envy, to have hasad — a spiritual disease involving wishing the removal of blessings from another
key_terms.يَقْفُو أَثَرَهُ: To follow in one's footsteps/tracks — here meaning the hypocrite surveils and monitors the believer
key_terms.يَنْفَكُّ: To be free from, to escape, to cease
key_terms.يُصَدَّقُ: To be believed/credited — passive form indicating social trust given to the envious believer's words

ai.seo_question: What four trials must every believer endure according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) describes four inescapable trials every believer faces: harm from a neighbor, temptation from a devil, surveillance from a hypocrite, and envy from a fellow believer. Remarkably, the Imam identifies the envious believer as the most dangerous of all — because a fellow Muslim's accusation carries social credibility and is readily believed by others. The conversation with Sama'a ibn Mihran, a trusted companion, underscores that this is a private teaching addressing the realities of communal life.
